extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners, patent attorneys/agents, and applicants involved in pre-AIA patent prosecution and novelty/derivation issues
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and overcoming rejections under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 (subsections (e), (f), and (g)) including requirements for priority/benefit claims, affidavits/declarations (37 CFR 1.131/1.132), inventorship/derivation, and when filing dates vs. conception/reduction-to-practice govern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional application must describe subject matter relied upon
rubrics_metrics.description: The provisional application must also describe, in compliance with pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, or 35 U.S.C. 112(a), the subject matter relied upon in the reference patent or publication to make the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2136, examples 2, 4, and 7. A provisional that does not sufficiently describe the subject matter (in compliance with written description/enablement requirements) cannot support using the earlier filing date for prior art purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on using international applications to 'reach back'
rubrics_metrics.description: International applications which (1) were filed prior to November 29, 2000, or (2) did not designate the U.S., or (3) were not published in English under PCT Article 21(2) by WIPO, may not be used to reach back (bridge) to an earlier filing date through a priority or benefit claim for prior art purposes under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners and practitioners must check filing dates, designations, and publication status/language before treating an international application as antedating prior art under pre-AIA 102(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefit of U.S. parent filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120
rubrics_metrics.description: A U.S. patent or patent application publication that claims the benefit of an earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120 will be accorded the earlier filing date as its prior art date under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), provided the earlier-filed application properly supports the subject matter relied upon in any rejection in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In other words, subject matter used in a rejection must be disclosed in the earlier-filed application in compliance with written description/enablement requirements in order to be entitled to the earlier filing date. See MPEP § 2136 and examples referenced in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference effective date is filing date (not conception/reduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: For prior art purposes under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), the effective date of the reference is its filing date in the United States; the date that the prior art subject matter was conceived or reduced to practice is of no importance when pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) is not at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When not in interference, use the filing date (including certain international filing dates) as the prior art date. See MPEP §§ 2120.01 and 2136. Do not rely on inventor's conception/reduction dates to antedate a 102(e) reference unless 102(g) or derivation issues apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'by another' — different inventive entity
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Another' means other than applicants — i.e., a different inventive entity. The inventive entity is different if not all inventors are the same; the fact that the application and reference have one or more inventors in common is immaterial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inventive entity differs, the reference may be treated as 'by another' under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e). See In re Land and Ex parte DesOrmeaux. The existence of shared inventors does not automatically make the reference not 'by another.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Different inventive entity is prima facie evidence reference is 'by another' (Milburn rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A U.S. patent, U.S. patent application publication or international application publication by a different inventive entity, whether or not the application shares some inventors in common with the patent, is prima facie evidence that the invention was made 'by another' as set forth in pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle (Milburn rule) is grounded in legislative history. See cited cases In re Mathews, In re Facius, and Ex parte DesOrmeaux. Examiners should treat a different inventive entity as prima facial evidence of 'by another' but consider rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods to overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection by: (A) persuasively arguing claims are patentably distinguishable; (B) amending the claims to patentably distinguish; (C) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing the reference invention is not by 'another'; (D) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) showing prior invention (in limited circumstances); (E) submitting and perfecting a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d); and/or (F) submitting a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 and establishing the prior application satisfies 35 U.S.C. 112 enablement/written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate method depending on the nature of the reference and available evidence. See MPEP §§ 2132.01, 2133.02(a), 715, 716.10, and the specific subsections referenced for details on timing, content, and limits (e.g., when 1.131 is or is not permitted, and written description/enablement requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Antedating a 102(e) reference via 37 CFR 1.131 (prior invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior U.S. patent, U.S. patent application publication, or international application publication that is not a statutory bar may be antedated by submitting an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 showing invention of the claimed subject matter by the inventor (or at least one joint inventor) prior to the effective date of the reference relied upon in the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 1.131 affidavit is not appropriate if the claims of the reference and the application are directed to the same invention or obvious variants — then interference or double-patenting issues may apply. See MPEP § 715 and § 2136.05(b) for when to use 1.131 vs 1.132.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for claiming foreign priority (35 U.S.C. 119) and benefit claims (35 U.S.C. 119(e)/120)
rubrics_metrics.description: To antedate a reference, an applicant can: (A) submit a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) within the time in 37 CFR 1.55 and establish that the prior foreign application satisfies enablement and written description of 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/pre-AIA 112 first paragraph; or (B) submit a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 within 37 CFR 1.78 and establish the prior application satisfies 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/pre-AIA 112 first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For applications filed on/after Sept 16, 2012, a corrected application data sheet under 37 CFR 1.76 identifying the prior application is often required; for earlier applications, specification amendments or oath/declaration techniques may be needed. Certified priority documents (and English translations when necessary) must be filed to perfect the priority date. Failure to perfect the priority/benefit claim prevents using that earlier date to antedate a reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 to show reference is inventor's own work
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 can overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection by showing the relied-on reference describes an inventor's or at least one joint inventor's own work (i.e., the reference is not 'by another').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 1.132 declaration cannot be a naked assertion of inventorship — it must provide context, explanation, or evidence to support the claim (see EmeraChem Holdings v. Volkswagen example of insufficiency). Proof may include showing association (same assignee) and that the inventor learned of the inventor's work from the inventor directly/indirectly. See MPEP §§ 715.01(a), 715.01(c), 716.10 and § 2136.05(b) for required contents and uses of 1.132 affidavits.

rubrics_metrics.name: When diligence/reduction-to-practice not required (reference is applicant's own work)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the reference reflects an inventor's or at least one joint inventor's own work, evidence of diligence or reduction to practice is not required to establish that the inventor invented the subject matter disclosed in the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A showing that the reference disclosure arose from the inventor's work coupled with a showing of conception by the inventor before the filing date of the reference (e.g., via a 1.132 affidavit and supporting exhibits) will overcome a pre-AIA 102(e) rejection. See In re DeBaun example and related discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claims in reference do not prove inventorship of individual elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of combination claims in a reference is not evidence that the inventor or at least one joint inventor invented individual elements or subcombinations included in that combination if those elements/subcombinations are not separately claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case law (In re DeBaun, In re Facius, In re Mathews) when evaluating whether a reference inventor actually invented an unclaimed subcomponent; a declaration of non-inventorship that is vague or addresses only a generic concept may be insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) — correctness of inventorship and derivation bar
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) bars issuance of a patent where an applicant did not himself invent the subject matter sought to be patented. The examiner must presume applicants are the proper inventors unless evidence of derivation exists; if it can be shown the inventor derived the invention from another, a 102(f) rejection is proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In uncommon situations where the application clearly names incorrect inventorship and no correction under 37 CFR 1.48 has been requested, the examiner should reject under 102(f). See cases such as In re VerHoef and Pannu v. Iolab. Attribution affidavits under 37 CFR 1.132 and related procedures are discussed in MPEP §§ 715.01 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation requires complete conception by another and communication to the deriver
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivation requires that another party completely conceive the invention and communicate that conception to the alleged deriver prior to any date on which the deriver possessed knowledge of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The communication must be sufficient to enable one of ordinary skill in the art to construct and successfully operate the invention (Kilbey v. Thiele; Hedgewick v. Akers; Gambro Lundia AB v. Baxter). Examiners look for evidence of enabling communication when assessing derivation claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party alleging derivation need not prove actual reduction to practice or U.S. derivation site
rubrics_metrics.description: The party alleging derivation does not have to prove an actual reduction to practice in order to show derivation; derivation of public knowledge or derivation occurring outside the U.S. can be sufficient to bar a deriver from patenting under pre-AIA 102(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Scott v. Brandenburger and Ex parte Andresen. Reduction to practice is not a prerequisite to proving derivation, though other elements (complete conception and enabling communication) remain required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation versus priority — distinct legal inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivation addresses originality (who invented the subject matter), whereas priority focuses on which party first invented the subject matter. They are related but legally distinct inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use derivation analysis to determine correct inventorship (102(f)) and priority/diligence analysis under 102(g) or interference contexts where dates of conception and reduction to practice and reasonable diligence matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) — actual reduction to practice and no abandonment/suppression
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) bars issuance of a patent where another made the invention in the United States before applicant and had not abandoned, suppressed, or concealed it. To qualify as prior art under 102(g), there must be evidence that the subject matter was actually reduced to practice; conception alone is not sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 102(g) issues arise in interference practice and may also form the basis for ex parte rejections if actual reduction to practice by another is shown without abandonment/suppression/concealment. See cited cases (Amgen v. Chugai; New Idea v. Sperry; E.I. DuPont v. Phillips; Kimberly-Clark v. Johnson & Johnson) and related MPEP chapters on interferences.
